weaknesses.statement: The 2-call item phase assumes ONE browser.job_status lands after the job has already finished. Every extra poll is +1 call and +191 B.
weaknesses.detail: A run that polls while the job is still traversing pays more calls for the same records; see the poll-sensitivity table.

weaknesses.statement: MAX_INLINE_BATCH_ITEMS is 2, so anything above 2 URLs is a job. The +1 poll is not an edge case — it is what every real traversal pays.
weaknesses.detail: The threshold is floor((45000 - 2250) / 15000), charging each item a SNAPSHOT_TIMEOUT_MS ceiling rather than an expected cost. Raising the per-item estimate to something measured would raise the inline batch size and delete the poll; nothing here measures it.

weaknesses.statement: The search call returns 40 of 240 rows, not 240 compacted rows. It is a smaller ANSWER as well as a smaller payload.
weaknesses.detail: All 240 rows in one call is 59769 B (still 62.5% under the uncompacted page); paging to 240 at the default window is 6 calls, which would make this phase MORE calls than the before surface's 2.

weaknesses.statement: On a small page compaction ADDS bytes: the eBay fixture goes 898 → 963 B and the Kijiji fixture 972 → 989 B.
weaknesses.detail: matchedCount/returnedCount/offset/hasMore/nextOffset/compacted, plus finalUrl and navigationStatus, are a fixed envelope only a long page amortises. The win is a function of row count and href length.

weaknesses.statement: Most of the preamble reduction is dashboard.feed mode "ids", which existed before Phase 2 and which the before run simply did not use.
weaknesses.detail: ids alone: 80.8% off the full feed. filter{active} + fields add 57.8% on top of that, and only the second figure is Phase 2's.

weaknesses.statement: The 5 shell calls and the 3 recovery snapshots the 2026-08-29 run spent are NOT counted as saved anywhere in this ledger.
weaknesses.detail: Both would need something this box does not have — the client's spill threshold, and a page that fails the way live ones do. See unmeasurable after.spill_avoided and after.recovery_calls.

weaknesses.statement: Compaction is agent-side work the Phase 1 surface did not do; the seconds column shows it on this box and cannot transfer it to the Windows one.
weaknesses.detail: Bytes were traded for CPU on the machine that owns the browser. The trade looks right, but only one side of it is measured here.

weaknesses.statement: The seconds column is extractor + compactor CPU measured in two different Node processes; differences under ~10 ms are noise, not findings.
weaknesses.detail: End-to-end wall time is unmeasurable here (no Chrome, no paired agent, no network). See unmeasurable call.wall_time.end_to_end.

probes.question: And if the routine insists on all 240 rows in one call?

detail.note: Canonical URLs and the field projection alone, with no window. This is the honest ceiling for "one call, whole page": the 40-row default is a smaller number because it is a smaller answer.

probes.question: And over the checked-in fixture, where nothing is constructed?

detail.note: Two candidates with bare /itm/<id>?hash=abc hrefs — almost no tracking payload to strip. Compaction makes this page BIGGER, not smaller: matchedCount/returnedCount/offset/hasMore/nextOffset/compacted plus finalUrl and navigationStatus are a fixed envelope cost that a two-row page cannot amortise. The win is a function of row count and href length, and this fixture has neither.

probes.question: What does one item cost as a compact batch slot instead of a full extract?

detail.note: compactItemRecord() drops the per-field provenance/confidence envelope, which is what makes a record auditable and also most of its size. A batch keeps the flat scoring fields; the full record is still one browser.extract away.

probes.question: What does the call that starts a promoted batch return?

detail.note: Zero result slots. This is why the poll below is a structural cost of the after surface and not an optional extra: a promoted batch hands back a jobId, and nothing else, in the call that starts it.

probes.question: And what does the poll that collects it return?

detail.note: Real BatchJobStore and real jobProgress(); the seventeen slots are seventeen copies of the one checked-in item fixture, exactly as the before ledger replays seventeen copies of the same extract. A real batch of seventeen different listings would differ per slot.

probes.question: What does one MORE poll cost, once the results are already read?

detail.note: sinceIndex is what makes over-polling cheap rather than free: a poll that has nothing new still costs its progress envelope, and that is the marginal price of each extra poll in the sensitivity table.

unmeasurable.reason: www.ebay.ca answers this box with HTTP 403 (bot wall); no live 240-row SRP can be fetched or extracted here.
The threshold above which the chat client spills a tool response to a file lives in the client, not in the gateway or the agent. Nothing in this repo observes it.
Real per-call latency is Chrome navigation plus the gateway-to-agent WebSocket round trip on a paired Windows box. No agent and no Chrome here; the seconds reported below are extractor CPU only.
The 5 shell calls that parsed the spilled search response were client-side tool calls against a local file. They are not gateway calls and leave no trace this repo can read.
browser.snapshot serializes a live accessibility tree; it has no fixture and no offline path.
The deals dashboard API is not reachable from this box and the harness holds no ingest token. The feed below is modelled at the reported size; only the mode-to-mode reduction is measured.

A 17-URL batch promotes to a job (MAX_INLINE_BATCH_ITEMS is 2), and how many browser.job_status polls a real run spends is the job's wall-clock duration — 17 live Chrome navigations — divided by the caller's polling cadence. Neither exists on this box. The ledger charges the structural floor of 1 poll and prints a sensitivity table; it does not predict the real number.
BATCH_JOB_DEADLINE_MS (375 s) and BATCH_ITEM_BUDGET_MS (15 s) are catalog ceilings used to decide promotion, not measurements of how long a traversal takes. Nothing here times a real batch.

The before run spent 5 shell calls parsing a search response the chat client had spilled to a file. The compacted response is ~13x smaller, but whether that clears the client's spill threshold is not knowable here — the threshold itself is unmeasurable (see client.inline_response_limit) — so those 5 calls are NOT counted as saved anywhere in this ledger.

Compaction moves work onto the agent: the seconds column charges the compactor's CPU on this box, which is not the CPU of the Windows box that would actually run it. The direction is real (the agent does strictly more work per call); the magnitude is not transferable.

Per-URL error slots are meant to remove the extra calls a dead page cost the Phase 1 traversal (the reported run spent 3 snapshots on ended listings reported active). Costing that saving needs a page that fails the way live ones do; every fixture here succeeds, so the saving is described and never counted.
